content: Cystic acne, also referred to as nodulocystic acne, represents a severe variant of acne in which inflammatory lesions develop into small cyst-like structures. These acne cysts are not true cysts in the pathological sense, as they do not involve abnormal dilations of skin structures. Instead, they are inflamed nodules. While cystic acne is not uncommon, it is less prevalent compared to other forms of acne. The condition arises due to an excessive accumulation of sebum within the pores. Contrary to widespread misconceptions, cystic acne is neither caused nor influenced by personal hygiene or the lack thereof. A widely used and effective treatment for cystic acne is isotretinoin, which achieves a cure in approximately 90% of patients. Cystic acne can manifest on various parts of the body, including the face, chest, back, shoulders, and, in some cases, the upper arms. Similar to common pimples, these cysts are typically filled with a white, pus-like substance. However, they are larger, often measuring several centimeters in diameter, and can be significantly painful. If left untreated, particularly without the use of antibiotics in combination with topical therapies, cystic acne frequently leads to scarring. The severity of scarring depends on the individual case, and while many scars can be treated, scars on the body tend to respond less favorably to treatment compared to those on the face. Complete removal of all scars is generally unlikely. After the resolution of most cysts, macules, or pseudo scars, may develop. These macules are red patches of skin that sometimes appear slightly raised and are located where the cysts previously existed. They can resemble true scars but are not permanent. Unlike actual scars, macules typically resolve within six months and do not leave lasting marks.
